title: Sale record: The Widow's Supper, 1952
chunk_text: Bill of sale dated 14 March 1952. The painting The Widow's Supper, oil on canvas, attributed to Cornelis van Leyden, was sold to the museum through the dealer Aert de Wilde of The Hague, acting on behalf of a family that asked to remain anonymous. The price paid was the highest the museum had ever spent on a single Dutch picture. The bill names no earlier owner and refers only to 'an old Dutch family collection'.

title: Letter of endorsement by Dr. Abraham Verhulst
chunk_text: Letter from Dr. Abraham Verhulst, the leading authority on Leiden painting of the later seventeenth century, to the museum board, February 1952: 'I have no hesitation in calling this the masterpiece of Cornelis van Leyden. The gravity of the figures and the handling of light on the cloth are his alone.' Verhulst examined the painting for one afternoon at the dealer's premises and did not see any technical examination.

title: Provenance search report
chunk_text: Report of the museum registrar, 1953. A search of auction catalogues, estate inventories and exhibition records from 1650 to 1950 found no mention of a supper scene by Cornelis van Leyden in any family collection. The dealer declined to name the family. The registrar notes that the painting has no recorded history at all before its appearance at the dealer's in 1951.

title: Dealer file: Aert de Wilde
chunk_text: Internal file on the dealer Aert de Wilde, compiled 1955. Trained as a painter in the 1920s, de Wilde exhibited his own work in the 1930s to poor reviews before turning to dealing. Between 1951 and 1955 he brought three 'newly discovered' seventeenth-century Dutch paintings to market, each from an unnamed family collection, each praised by Dr. Verhulst.

title: Pre-sale condition note
chunk_text: Condition note written by the museum's restorer before purchase, 1952. 'The paint surface is unusually hard and resists the usual solvents; a cotton swab with alcohol had no effect even in the darks. The crack pattern is regular and the cracks appear filled with a dark deposit. Varnish removal was not attempted.' The note was filed and not discussed by the board.

title: Cornelis van Leyden: life and works
chunk_text: Reference entry. Cornelis van Leyden (c. 1630-1702), Leiden painter of quiet interior scenes, of whom fewer than a dozen works are known. His death inventory of 1702 lists 'a supper piece with a widow, unfinished'. No such painting was known until 1951; the entry was widely cited as proof that The Widow's Supper is the lost work.

title: Auction catalogue entry, lot 27
chunk_text: Evening sale of modern art, November 2003, lot 27. Heinrich Moll, Blue Horses at Dusk, 1914, oil on canvas, signed lower right. Provenance: Werner Jaeger collection, Krefeld, acquired directly from the artist; by descent to the present owner. The stretcher bears a label of the Galerie Sturmhaus, Dusseldorf. Sold for a record price for the artist.

title: Heinrich Moll catalogue raisonne, entry 1914/12
chunk_text: Catalogue raisonne of Heinrich Moll, 1968, entry 1914/12: 'Blue Horses at Dusk. Oil on canvas. Listed in the artist's own handlist of 1914. Whereabouts unknown, presumed lost; no photograph exists.' The entry was quoted in the 2003 catalogue as confirming the painting's existence.

title: Galerie Sturmhaus stock books: search result
chunk_text: Letter from the archive holding the surviving Galerie Sturmhaus stock books, 2012. The books for 1912-1920 survive complete and record no painting by Moll with horses. The archive adds that the label on the stretcher differs in typeface and paper from every authenticated Sturmhaus label in its collection.

title: Letter from the consignor
chunk_text: Letter from the consignor to the auction house, 2003. He writes that his grandfather Werner Jaeger bought the painting from Moll in 1914 and kept it hidden through two wars. He has no receipt, photograph or correspondence, explaining that family papers were lost in 1943. He has sold several other works 'from the Jaeger collection' since 1995.

title: Expert certificate
chunk_text: Certificate issued in 2003 by a specialist in German expressionism: 'Blue Horses at Dusk is an authentic and important work by Heinrich Moll, entirely characteristic of his palette in 1914.' The certificate is based on photographs and one viewing; no technical analysis was commissioned before the sale.

title: Heinrich Moll: life and works
chunk_text: Reference entry. Heinrich Moll (1880-1916), German expressionist painter of animals in non-naturalistic colour, killed at Verdun in March 1916. His productive years were 1910-1914; after August 1914 he was at the front and painted almost nothing. Many works listed in his 1914 handlist are lost.

title: Letter to Theo, Saint-Remy, June 1889
chunk_text: In a letter to his brother Theo written at the Saint-Remy asylum around 2 June 1889, Vincent van Gogh wrote: 'This morning I saw the countryside from my window a long time before sunrise, with nothing but the morning star, which looked very big.' Letters from the following weeks mention a new study of a starry sky.

title: Provenance summary
chunk_text: After the artist's death the painting passed to Johanna van Gogh-Bonger, who sold it in 1900. It went through private collections in France and the Netherlands, was acquired by a Rotterdam collector in 1906, and was sold through a Paris and New York dealer in 1938. It entered a New York museum in 1941 through an exchange funded by a bequest.

title: Asylum record, Saint-Paul-de-Mausole
chunk_text: Vincent van Gogh was admitted to the asylum of Saint-Paul-de-Mausole at Saint-Remy-de-Provence on 8 May 1889 and left in May 1890. He was given a second room as a studio. The view east from his bedroom window over a walled wheat field towards the hills appears in many of his paintings from that year.

title: Anonymous letter to the museum
chunk_text: Anonymous typed letter received in 1998 claiming that 'the real Starry Night was copied in Rotterdam around 1906 and the copy is the one you own'. The letter names no copyist and gives no evidence. The museum logged it with other unsolicited claims; no follow-up is recorded.
